questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to experience a big and exciting city in a country with cultural differences to Denmark, and which I didn't know much about.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would highly recommend anyone taking a semester abroad. Budapest is an excellent city for studying as it has a rich history, diverse culture, affordable living, and a lively social scene filled with young people, including many international students. Living independently in a new country and meeting people from around the globe was an amazing experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy, the university, ELTE, provides all the information you need.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Plenty of assistance, as this is also provided by ELTE by mail and in person during the first weeks of school.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was easy to find housing. ELTE informs you of several websites that rents out flats, and there are many good and cheap options.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I didn't meet anyone who chose on-campus housing, as it was both cheap and convenient to find off-campus options in Budapest's best areas. I highly recommend finding a place on the Pest side near the school, as that's where you'll spend most of your time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The apartments are often very large, but not always well-isolated so could become very cold in the winter.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was very easy to navigate the registration course, especially with help from the coordinator and/or mentors.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was divided in two parts: you register for the courses you wish based on a list from the university's website, which has detailed information on the courses and their exams. They use the system, Neptun. If you don't get the ones you want you can re-register in the second round, and you can also do this if you change your mind about one or several of the courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The coordinators and mentors were very available to help with the process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes i wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Check the courses beforehand, also in regard to the timetables to make sure they don't overlap. The coordinator will make it really simple for you to have an overview over this, so don't stress about it. You can probably also manage to switch courses during the first days of school.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The courses were all 5 ECTS meaning you have to take 6 courses. It was completely manageable, but worth planning your schedule based on not choosing courses with exams that are overlapping.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was actually higher than I had expected, and the professors was really competent and good at teaching. However, some of the classes were a bit chaotic and less structured than what I was used to at UCPH, and because the courses are so "small" most of them will be more superficial than at UCPH. The exams was much easier, being mostly essays on self-chosen topics or short in-class written exams.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was similar to UCPH, and varied from class to class. Most classes followed a lecture format, with teachers presenting the syllabus using PowerPoint. However, some courses emphasized in-class participation, group work, and presentations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Consumer Protection, International Criminal Law, European Private Law, Childrens' rights in the EU law and Policy, Fundamental Rights Before Courts & EU Human Rights and Criminal Justice.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: International Criminal Law was very interesting and was run by passionated teachers. EU Human Rights and Criminal Justice was my favourite class, as it was 5 hours every other Friday, which gave time for in depth work on the subjects. The teacher was highly competent and good at creating in-class discussions.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My rent was much higher, as I lived alone and in a very central neighborhood. I also traveled much more than I expected, the costs of which are not included in the above. I would recommend to factor in this as you probably will travel a lot to many of the nice places close to Budapest.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Supermarkets were more expensive than I thought. Transportation was extremely cheap, less than 2000 HUF for a monthly pass to travel through entire Hungary.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were many sports courses available as well as a free trial week for trying out any you were interested in. The Erasmus organizations also planned several social activities for any taste on a daily basis.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend to sign up for a sports course like Volleyball, to meet other people, or pilates or spinning as exercise. It's a good way to meet people and to experience a new hobby.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend to spend weekends and holidays exploring the city or other small, but beautiful, towns of Hungary. Many amazing places is also only a train ride away like Slovenia, Prague and Vienna. But Budapest is big and very active, so you will not be bored!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't socialize much with local students, but, as mentioned, joining a sport will guarantee you to meet locals. It was also nice to go bars that were not touristic (you will not meet them at Szimpla Kert).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The elder people speak non to very little English, which could be challenging but not a big problem. Hungary is in general a more conservative country than Denmark, and though I didn't have any negative experiences myself, it was something I was aware of. Even though the people of Budapest seemed much more open-minded, and there are many pride-friendly places, it is worth noting the Hungarian laws on homosexuality ect. before you arrive.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Budapest is a beautiful city to walk around in and the way it looks today bears the mark of a long history (such as the ruin bars and thermal baths). Today, it is very multicultural and has something for every taste.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
First, the university is very helpful and will do a lot to make you comfortable.
Second, they have a lot of interesting courses and competent teachers and the university of ELTE is in general more "open" than I would have expected from a country like Hungary.
Third, it's a big city that offers many fun experiences if you are open to look for them

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I met only one other student from Denmark, so it might be worth knowing that Budapest is not a common exchange destination for Danish students. However, it is for many other countries, so it's not a problem to meet kind people and get friends!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people i met was the best part of the experience, but it was also really rewarding to become more independent and learn to live on your own outside of the comfort of your own familiar country.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: In general it was no too challenging, but the greatest challenge was probably the practical preparation and registration process. However, it was not as difficult as I feared.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
